newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. urges Milosevic to talk to opposition.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Milosevic to talk to opposition.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Monday urged Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to open a dialogue with the opposition and said NATO would take "unified action" to hammer home that message.

Christopher, speaking on the eve of a NATO foreign ministers' meeting, called Milosevic's refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections "self-defeating" and said he should change his stance "in his own self-interest".

The Secretary of State also told a news conference he would raise the issue of Serbia at a meeting in Brussels on Tuesday with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in an attempt to shift Moscow away from its support for Milosevic.

Christopher's comments marked another step in mounting U.S. outrage over Serbian authorities' decision to annul sweeping victories for an opposition alliance in local polls on November 17. A Serbian court on Saturday rejected five appeals by the opposition.
"The United States has left no doubt and I leave no doubt about our support for democratic change in Serbia," Christopher said.

"We've urged Milosevic, have been and continue to, to open dialogue with the opposition, recognise the importance of freedom of assembly, to accept the results of the election and especially to preserve freedom of the media."
Christopher said he also wanted to emphasise again to Milosevic the importance of not using force against opposition demonstrations which have taken place daily for the last three weeks in Serbia.

"I think that's the only prudent course for him to follow," Christopher said. "I would hope and expect that there would be a unified action on the part of NATO members reflecting the comments that I've just made."
The secretary of state did not say what action was expected but appeared to be referring to a joint statement or proposal.

He said Milosevic, whose role Washington has acknowledged in helping to negotiate last year's Dayton peace accord in Bosnia, had shown himself in the past to be pragmatic and flexible and was capable of changing position now.
Christopher said that in his meeting with Primakov he wanted to emphasise "that I believe that Milosevic's position at the present time is self-defeating".
He said one issue he would raise was the possibility of U.N. action to renew sanctions against Serbia that were lifted after the Dayton accord.
Washington has said it retains the right to seek such action, but U.S. officials have played down the likelihood of it, acknowledging likely opposition from Russia and others in the Security Council.
Discouraged by Saturday's court action in Belgrade, U.S. officials expressed gloom about Milosevic's handling of the Serbian crisis.

"He's not showing as much flexibility as he ought to. He is not taking up our strong urging and constructive suggestions about how to deal with it, and I think he's digging himself in, which is a very bad sign for him and for his country," one said.

The official, who asked not to be identified, speculated that the reason Milosevic had not so far authorised strong-arm tactics against the demonstrators was because he was afraid of drawing workers into the protests.
But he said: "What we are doing is saying if he doesn't clean up his act that he will be in very deep trouble, and we have to anticipate that."
